doc.title: Zeke Mullins interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 9, 2017

title: Chord substitutions and bandleaders who resist them
summary: How substitute chords and extended chords work, and how some leaders object to altered changes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Right. But you’ve got to learn the scales because you were taking classical lessons.
I’ve often wondered, part of being a jazz piano player is doing substitution chords sometimes.
Do you have a method, or can you explain how you choose to switch out one chord for another?

Well each chord has a substitute neighbor, and you can go from this. And once you learn the what you call foundational chord, you find out, what is the neighbor, what is this called, what is this called. And you go from that. And that way you can find out how to use your substitute chord. It’s not done overnight. It takes quite a little while to really absorb that and be proficient enough to do it. You know, if you become familiar with an arrangement and you don’t like a chord in there, well now you can substitute something for it but it has to be something harmonically within the arrangement you know. It’s the same thing with adding, in other words, adding notes to chords. You know, building, stretching chords out. You have to know when to do this and when not to.
And does it depend on who you are playing behind?

Sometimes, yes. Because some musicians, some band leaders or whatever, they don’t want to hear — they’re used to hearing a certain chord. “Hey, man, why you playing that, man? Don’t play that.” And they’ll tell you what they want to hear, you know, because they’ve been hearing this for God knows how long you know. But that used to bug me in a way because sometimes some of the chord changes, to me, to my ear, they seemed kind of dull you know. And I studied how to lengthen, how to add on notes. And “No man, don’t play that.” That used to annoy me. But I kind of laid back on it you know. But some guys would want you to do that. You know, would want you to add on or change some notes. Because it gives the particular arrangement, it gives it a different sound.
Yeah. It lets the improviser sort of go a little —
